lead.t: Chronic kidney disease reduces EPO → normocytic, low‑retic anaemia. — In CKD the appropriate next step is to assess renal function and consider erythropoiesis‑stimulating agents.

snip.t: Chronic kidney disease reduces EPO → normocytic, low‑retic anaemia. — In CKD the appropriate next step is to assess renal function and consider erythropoiesis‑stimulating agents.

| Chronic kidney disease anaemia | Normocytic, low retic, low serum EPO, elevated creatinine, often accompanied by hypertension or proteinuria. | Low EPO level measured; improvement with erythropoiesis‑stimulating agents. |
Anaemia Management: Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs) and iron supplementation.
Pallor (conjunctivae, palms): Reduced hemoglobin from ineffective erythropoiesis.
Jaundice or scleral icterus (mild): Ineffective erythropoiesis leads to intramedullary hemolysis and bilirubin rise.
• Treat anaemia (erythropoiesis‑stimulating agent, iron supplementation) — Target Hb 10–12 g/dL; avoid hypertension
Nutritional deficiencies (vit B12, folate): Impair erythropoiesis, aggravate anaemia

qs.q: Which cytokine is noted to inhibit erythropoiesis and transferrin synthesis while stimulating fever and granulopoiesis?
qs.e: Interleukin-1 (IL-1) stimulates fever, granulopoiesis, and synthesis of acute-phase reactants while directly inhibiting erythropoiesis and transferrin synthesis. Other cytokines have distinct primary roles.

qs.q: What is a major clinical consequence of ineffective erythropoiesis and intramedullary expansion in beta thalassemia major?
o: Premature closure of all cranial sutures
Cortical bone thickening of the long bones
Skeletal deformities of the skull and maxilla
qs.e: Erythroid hyperplasia with intramedullary expansion and cortical bone thinning leads to skeletal deformities of the skull and maxilla. This can necessitate surgical or orthodontic correction.

qs.q: Which serum enzyme activity is markedly elevated in megaloblastic anemia as a direct marker of ineffective erythropoiesis?
qs.e: Serum activity of lactate dehydrogenase is markedly elevated in megaloblastic anemia, serving as a marker of ineffective erythropoiesis. Other enzymes do not reflect intramedullary red cell destruction as directly.

qs.q: Which cytokine stimulates granulopoiesis, thrombopoiesis, fever, and the synthesis of acute-phase reactants while inhibiting erythropoiesis?
qs.e: Interleukin-1 stimulates fever, granulopoiesis, thrombopoiesis, and synthesis of proteins like ferritin, CRP, and fibrinogen while inhibiting erythropoiesis. Other interleukins do not share this exact profile outlined in the chronic disease pathways.

qs.q: In healthy adults, the principal site of erythropoiesis is:
qs.e: Normal adult erythropoiesis occurs predominantly in red bone marrow.

qs.q: The major site of erythrocyte production (erythropoiesis) in humans after birth is the:
qs.e: In adults, the bone marrow, particularly the red marrow of flat bones and the epiphyses of long bones, is the primary site of red blood cell production.
qs.s: Weekly Year 2: Cellular Immunology Exam - June 5, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: In adult humans, the major physiological site of erythrocyte production (erythropoiesis) is which of the following?
qs.e: In adults, the red bone marrow is the primary site of hematopoiesis, including the production of erythrocytes. The liver and spleen can be sites of extramedullary hematopoiesis under certain pathological conditions.
qs.s: Weekly Year 2: Cellular Immunology Exam - May 1, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: In a healthy adult, what is the major site of erythrocyte production (erythropoiesis)?
qs.e: In adults, erythropoiesis occurs almost exclusively in the red bone marrow of flat and long bones.
qs.s: Weekly Year 2: Cellular Immunology Exam - April 3, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: Erythropoiesis is the bone‑marrow process that creates mature red blood cells. It integrates oxygen sensing, hormone signaling, and iron handling, and its failure produces anemia.

sections.p: Red blood cells are generated from multipotent hematopoietic stem cells in the erythroid lineage. The journey from a pro‑erythroblast to a reticulocyte takes about 7 days and yields ~2 million cells per second in a healthy adult.
b: Occurs in red marrow of flat bones and in the pelvis.
Each mature RBC carries ~270 million hemoglobin molecules.

sections.p: Stem cells commit to the erythroid line under the influence of transcription factors (GATA‑1, EKLF). Early progenitors proliferate, then undergo hemoglobin synthesis, nuclear condensation, and enucleation to become reticulocytes that enter circulation.
b: Iron is imported via transferrin‑receptor (CD71) and stored as ferritin.
Heme synthesis occurs partly in mitochondria (δ‑ALA → protoporphyrin IX).
Enucleation is assisted by macrophage ‘nurse cells’.

sections.p: Kidney peritubular cells sense arterial O₂ tension and release erythropoietin (EPO). EPO binds the EPO‑R on early erythroblasts, promoting survival and proliferation. Iron availability, hepcidin, and cytokines fine‑tune output.

t.b: Is the anemia due to inadequate hormonal drive? High in hypoxic states, low in renal failure.
Is iron supply sufficient? Low ferritin indicates true iron deficiency; high ferritin with low saturation suggests functional iron deficiency (e.g., inflammation).
Is the marrow responding? Low retic in aplastic or iron‑deficiency anemia; high retic in hemolysis or blood loss.

sections.p: Failure can be quantitative (decreased production) or qualitative (defective hemoglobin). Common mechanisms include iron deficiency, chronic disease, marrow infiltration, viral suppression, and inherited dyserythropoiesis.
b: Iron‑deficiency anemia – most common worldwide; diet‑poor or chronic blood loss.
Anemia of chronic disease – hepcidin‑mediated iron sequestration.
Aplastic crisis – parvovirus B19 transiently halts erythropoiesis, dangerous in sickle cell or thalassaemia.
Congenital dyserythropoietic anaemia – ineffective erythropoiesis with multinucleated erythroblasts.

sections.p: Understanding erythropoiesis guides work‑up of anemia, predicts response to therapy, and alerts clinicians to life‑threatening crises in hemolytic disorders.
b: A low retic count with microcytic anemia → iron deficiency or chronic disease.
A high retic count with normocytic anemia → hemolysis or acute blood loss.
Sudden drop in retics in a sickle‑cell child → parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis; urgent transfusion needed.

sections.p: Key points tested: stimulus for EPO, iron‑regulatory role of hepcidin, interpretation of reticulocyte index, and recognition of aplastic crisis in hemolytic disease.
b: EPO is produced mainly by renal peritubular fibroblasts.
Hepcidin rises with inflammation and blocks ferroportin.
Parvovirus B19 targets erythroid progenitors → aplastic crisis.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe anemia (Hb < 7 g/dL) with tachycardia or hypotension
Aplastic crisis in sickle‑cell disease (rapid Hb drop, retic < 1%)
Acute hemolysis with dark urine and jaundice

faq.q: Why does anemia of chronic disease have normal or high ferritin?
faq.a: Inflammation raises hepcidin, trapping iron in macrophages; ferritin reflects stored iron and is an acute‑phase reactant.

faq.q: Can vitamin B12 deficiency affect erythropoiesis?
faq.a: Yes, it impairs DNA synthesis, causing macrocytic anemia with ineffective erythropoiesis.

faq.q: What is the role of the spleen in erythropoiesis?
faq.a: The spleen removes abnormal or aged RBCs and provides a niche for late‑stage maturation of reticulocytes.

exam: Explain how hypoxia leads to increased red‑cell mass, naming the key hormone and its source.
